messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Martin, a 56-year-old European American man who had built his life around movement, came to therapy after more than a year of trying to live with the aftermath of a driving accident that had changed him and injured another person. He and his wife had been returning from an evening out when, at a turn he misjudged, his car struck a pedestrian crossing late in the dark. Martin had never before been in anything like it. He remembered the sickening thud, the sight of the other man on the pavement, and the sirens arriving while Martin stood frozen, certain he had ruined not only a stranger’s body but his own identity. As a dancer, he had always understood himself as precise, attentive, and responsible with other people’s bodies; after the accident, he felt that he had failed in the one role that mattered most to him. That belief settled quickly into a hard self-judgment: he would never forgive himself for not doing more to stop what happened, and he should have protected others and failed. 

In the months that followed, certain songs would catch him off guard and pull him back to the evening in a way that felt immediate rather than remembered. A familiar tune in a restaurant, or music playing softly in a shop, could suddenly make him picture the crash again and re-enter the moment of impact. Crowded spaces had a similar effect. When he was in a busy lobby, at a performance venue, or even on a packed sidewalk, the crush of bodies and noise made his mind jump to the chaos of that night and to the thought that he had been too slow, too careless, too little in control. Seeing a car hit by accident in a film, on the news, or even briefly on the street sharpened the same conviction: he had failed in his most important role in life. Each trigger seemed to feed the self-accusation, and the self-accusation in turn made the triggers more potent, because now the music, the crowding, and the crash images did not just remind him of the event; they seemed to confirm his moral failure. 

Trying to live with those thoughts, Martin began to manage his days by narrowing them. He avoided going to or near the place where the event happened, taking longer routes across town and turning down errands that would bring him close to that intersection. He tried hard not to think about the trauma, pushing the scene away whenever it rose into his mind. He also dwelled on how he used to be before the event, replaying the younger version of himself who moved with confidence through rehearsals and streets alike, as if comparison might explain what had been lost. But the effort to keep it out of awareness left him more strained rather than less. The more he suppressed, the more his mind seemed to stay on guard for any hint of the memory breaking through, and the more difficult it became to concentrate on anything else. He could no longer follow choreography as fluidly, would lose counts in rehearsal, and found himself unable to relax even when he knew he was in a safe place. At night he lay awake needing to stay alert, as if vigilance might prevent another disaster, but the cost was exhaustion and a constant sense that something terrible could happen again at any moment. 

By the time he sought help, the circle had tightened. Because he was so keyed up and unable to settle, ordinary stimuli became easier to misread as warnings, and songs, crowds, and any image of a collision could seize his attention before he had a chance to steady himself. His sleeping became more fragmented, his concentration worse, and he found himself living in a smaller and smaller world, with work and marriage both shaped by the effort to keep from being overwhelmed. Even in the studio where he once felt most alive, the sound system could become a threat if the wrong song came on, and he would tense, scan, and struggle to keep his composure in front of others. What finally brought Martin in was not a single new event but the realization that he could no longer keep the burden hidden from his wife or his company, and that his life had begun to organize itself around fear of his own thoughts. He said he was most afraid that he would never get back the man he used to be, yet he was also hoping that, with help, he might finally stop punishing himself long enough to sleep, work, and move through the world again.
